questions.stem: A client had sudden unilateral weakness and slurred speech that completely resolved within 30 minutes. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The episode is benign because the neurologic deficits resolved completely, so no urgent assessment is needed unless similar symptoms last longer the next time.","B":"The episode is most consistent with dehydration because transient focal weakness and dysarthria usually resolve after oral fluids without further evaluation.","C":"The episode can be managed as a routine outpatient complaint because transient neurologic symptoms do not meaningfully predict near-term stroke risk.","D":"The episode is consistent with a transient ischemic attack and requires urgent evaluation because transient symptoms can precede a completed ischemic stroke."}}
questions.rationale: Sudden focal weakness and dysarthria that resolve can represent a TIA, and the American Stroke Association advises emergency assessment even when symptoms disappear. Option D correctly identifies both the syndrome and urgency. Option A wrongly treats symptom resolution as reassurance. Option B substitutes dehydration for a focal neurologic event without evidence. Option C understates the near-term stroke risk and delays evaluation.
questions.source_name: American Stroke Association — Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
questions.source_detail: The American Stroke Association describes TIA as transient stroke-like symptoms that may resolve quickly but require emergency assessment because they warn of subsequent stroke risk.

qc.qc_note: Strict final audit: max/min option-character ratio <=1.15; keyed option within 10% of distractor mean; keyed option is neither shortest nor longest; distractors manually reviewed for clinical plausibility, grammatical parallelism, and answer-cue leakage.
